list.listitem: All finger and hand trauma require radiographic evaluation with posteroanterior, lateral, and oblique views. C

Treatment for distal phalanx extensor mechanism disruption (mallet finger) requires continuous splinting in extension for at least 6 weeks. All splints achieve similar results. Conservative treatment can be initiated despite delayed presentation up to 4 months. B
All suspected or confirmed flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) injuries (jersey finger) should be referred for surgical evaluation/correction. C
Fifth metacarpal neck (boxer's) fractures heal well no matter what treatment is employed if the angulation is less than 70º. B
Strongly suspect ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) injury (skier's thumb) if there is trauma and pain on the ulnar side of the base of the thumb. C

background.definition: Finger and hand trauma includes tendon and ligament injury or disruption, joint dislocation, bone bruising, and fractures. Correct diagnosis and treatment is required to ensure maximal functionality.

list.listitem: Hand injuries represent 1% of all emergency department visits in the United States, and 10% to 15% of all athletic injuries.
The peak incidence is between 10 and 19 years of age.
Finger and hand injuries represent the most common occupational work-related injuries and 10% of all fractures.
Distal phalanx extensor mechanism disruption (mallet finger) results from forced flexion of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint.
Flexor digitorum profundus injuries (jersey finger) results from forced extension of the DIP.
Acute ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) injury, also known as skier's thumb, results from forced abduction of the first metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint.
5th metacarpal neck (boxer's) fracture results from a blow to the distal portion of the fifth MCP.
All finger and hand trauma require radiographic evaluation: posteroanterior, lateral, and oblique views. C
Ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) injury or "Skier's thumb" should be considered with traumatic injury to the base of thumb and radiographs should be obtained prior to ligament testing. C

Mechanism of injury generally predicts the type of injury. Special maneuvers can confirm a diagnosis, but radiographs are recommended to rule out concomitant fracture even for suspected ligamentous injuries.

Mallet finger (Distal phalanx extensor injury): Caused by an object striking or a force applied to the distal phalanx forcing flexion. There is an inability to actively extend the distal phalanx. To test, you must isolate the DIP by holding the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) in full extension. If the clinician is unable to passively fully extend the DIP, then there is a mechanical block.

Jersey (FDP) finger: Caused by forced extension of distal phalanx. There is an inability to actively flex the DIP. To test you must isolate the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon by extending the affected finger and keeping the rest of the hand in a fist. Then, hold the PIP in extension and have the patient actively attempt to flex the DIP. No movement indicates disruption of the FDP.

Skier's (UCL) thumb: Suggested by pain at ulnar side of the thumb base after trauma. Obtain radiographs first to rule out a fracture. If there is a fracture do not perform any ligamentous stability testing. If no fracture is present, apply a valgus load to the first MCP to test the integrity of the ligament; any laxity indicates partial disruption.

Boxer's (5th metacarpal neck) fracture: Caused when the fist strikes an object and patient reports pain over the distal portion of the fifth metacarpal. Assess for angulation and rotation. Rotation can be ascertained by having the patient make a loose fist. All the fingernails should be on the same plane and point to the scaphoid. Any laceration associated with this injury strongly suggests a "fight bite".
Radiographs (posteroanterior, lateral and oblique view) are recommended to confirm diagnosis or more serious injury, or when there is the possibility of a foreign body.

Ultrasound is increasingly used at point of care and has good accuracy for digital fractures. In one study, 119 patients with injury to a proximal or middle phalanx was moderately accurate for diagnosis of fracture (LR+ 7.9, LR− 0.23). In addition ultrasound can aid in indentification of foreign bodies, and test for ligament and tendon integrity both statically and dynamically.
A systematic review of 7 studies with 842 participants found that ultrasound was 91% sensitive and 96% specific (LR+ 21, LR- 0.09) for detection of hand fractures.
Mallet finger (Distal phalanx extensor injury): Radiographs must be checked to rule out a concomitant fracture and an ultrasound can be considered to confirm integrity of the extensor mechansim.

Jersey (FDP) finger: Radiographs must be checked to rule out a concomitant fracture and an ultrasound can be considered to confirm integrity of the flexor digitorium profundus and if torn, the degree of retraction.
Skier's (UCL) thumb: Obtain radiographs first to rule out a fracture and an ultrasound can be considered to confirm the integrity of the ulnar collateral ligament.
Boxer's (5th metacarpal neck) fracture: Radiographs will confirm presence of a fracture.
See for an overview of diagnosis and treatment for each fracture.
Intra-articular fractures, especially those involving more than 1/3 of the articulating surface, should be referred.C
All types of splints used to treat mallet finger achieve similar results; patient compliance is the key factor in treatment success as splinting must be continious for 6 weeks. B
All suspected flexor tendon injuries (including all cases of jersey finger) should be referred. C
Boxer's fractures heal well regardless of reduction or splinting technique if the fracture is not more than 70º angulated and no rotation is present. B

Physical therapy is required and involves restoring range of motion and strength of the finger and hand, which can be done by squeezing a ball and fully exetnding the fingers and hands. Can be accomplished at home if patient can demonstrate understanding and compliance.
Use of a vapocoolant spray significantly reduces pain during digital nerve blocks.
A small study found that a low dose (1 ml = 50 mg) of intranasal ketamine was effective as an anesthetic during digital nerve block (pain score 28 vs 48).

Treat with a splint that keeps the DIP in extension continuously for 6 weeks, and for another 4 to 6 weeks when participating in athletic competition. Patient compliance is key, and splint changes should be observed in the office or with a competent partner. Be careful not to cause skin maceration or necrosis.

Even with proper treatment, up to 20% of patients will have some permanent flexion or extension lag of the DIP. Conservative treatment can be attempted even with a delay of up to 3 months and does not comprimise surgical outcomes.

A systematic review identified 39 observational studies and 5 RCTs comparing surgical with nonsurgical management of mallet finger, and found no clear difference in outcomes. This was confirmed in a second systematic review of 10 cohort studies and 3 RCTs.
These are all treated surgically. Refer to an orthopedic surgeon within 72 hours. Splint affected digit in flexion while awaiting surgical treatment.

If there is no fracture and there is minimal to no laxity in the ligament, the injury should be immobilized via a thumb-spica cast/splint for 6 weeks continuously and then for another 4 to 6 weeks while participating in athletic competition.

Any rotation requires manipulation to correct; if unfamiliar with this technique, referral is required. Fractures with angulation up to 70º heal similarly regardless of reduction or splinting used, but expert recommendation is to attempt anatomical reduction and to splint the affected finger in 70º to 90º of flexion, either with a commercial splint or formed cast/splint for 4 to 5 weeks.
Simple buddy tape the 5th digit to the 4th digit has been found to be an acceptable treatment option in a systematic review of 5 randomized trials.

A randomized trial of 126 adults (mostly male) with a closed 5th metacarpal fracture randomized them to buddy taping of the 4th and 5th fingers at the proximal and middle phalanges, with gauze separating the fingers, or to ulnar gutter cast. Patients with rotational deformity, tendon injury or fracture angulation >70 degrees were excluded. At 3 months, functional ability, pain, and quality of life scores were similar between groups.

A randomized trial of 40 patients with 5th metacarpal neck in children compared traditional ulnar gutter splint with a hand-based thermoplastic splint. Children treated with the ulnar gutter splint had decreased grip strength at 6 weeks, although long-term strength was not reported. The two groups had similar pain and function scores, although the study was small and likely underpowered.

A randomized trial of 90 patients with Boxer's fracture compared ulnar gutter slab with transverse pinning in fixation. Union occurred at 7.5 weeks in both groups, and there were no differences in functional outcomes.
Repeat radiography is recommended but the ideal interval has not been determined. Expert recommendation is to do so initially in 1 week and then prior to removing splint/cast.

A small trial randomized 42 patients wth displaced oblique or spiral metacarpal shaft fracture to operative treatment with screw fixation of nonoperative treatment with unrestricted mobilization. Functional outcomes were similar, while cost and sick leave duration were significantly shorter with nonoperative treatment.

Mallet finger (Distal phalanx extensor injury): Refer if unable to passively fully extend, failed conservative therapy or fracture involving more than 1/3 articulating surface. A meta-analysis of 8 studies with 362 patients (4 RCTs, 4 cohorts) found no clear difference in outcomes for Kirschner wire fixation versus suture anchor technique other than fewer reported complications with the Kirschner wire.
Jersey (FDP) finger: Refer all patients ideally with 72 hours but no later than 10 days.
Skier's (UCL) thumb: Refer if a fracture is present or there is laxity upon stress testing of the joint compared to the unaffected limb.
Boxer's (5th metacarpal neck) fracture: Refer if unable to correct rotation or if laceration is present
Any intra-articular fractures, especially those involving more than 1/3 of the articulating surface, should be referred.
High-level athletes or vocations that will not allow adequate splinting/casting should be referred to discuss surgical options.

Mallet finger: Patient compliance is the key factor. Splint changes should be observed and follow-up should be every 2 weeks until treatment is complete. Even with proper treatment, up to 20% of patients will have some permanent flexion or extension lag of the DIP. Conservative treatment can be attempted even with a delay of up to 4 months. B
Jersey finger: With prompt recognition and surgical consultation, satisfactory results are common. C
Skier's(UCL) thumb: If complete tears and fractures are recoginized and treated properly, outcomes are good. C
Boxer's (5th metacarpal neck) fracture: Tend to do well regardless of the treatment provided the angulation is less than 70º and no rotation. C
Maintain a high index of suspicion for growth plate injuries and consider referral if you are inexperienced in the treatment of this population.

feature.caption: Management of Common Finger Fractures.
feature.feature_body:
Injury Key Examination Findings Treatment Referral Criteria
Extensor tendon injury at the DIP joint (mallet finger) Tender at dorsal aspect of the DIP joint Splint the DIP joint in extension continuously for 6 weeks Avulsion fracture involving more than 1/3 of the joint or inability to achieve full passive extension
No active extension of the DIP joint
FDP tendon injury (jersey finger) Tender at volar aspect of the DIP joint Refer to orthopedic surgeon All
Inability to flex the DIP joint
DIP should be isolated during the examination
5th Metacarpal bone fracture (boxer's fracture) Determine extent of angulation, evaluate for rotation Administer ulnar or hematoma block and attempt reduction Any rotation or angulation of more than 70º
Buddy tape/splinting/casting should last 4-5 weeks Presence of laceration
Follow up with radiography to ensure proper healing
Disruption of UCL at the thumb (skier's thumb) Pain at UCL. Test for joint stability only if fracture ruled out (anesthesia may be required) Immobilize stable joint in thumb spica cast/splint for 6 weeks Fracture or unstable joint
PIP, proximal interphalangeal; MCP, metacarpophalangeal; DIP, distal interphalangeal; FDP, flexor digitorum profundus; UCL, ulnar collateral ligament. Adapted from Leggit JC, Meko CJ. Acute finger injuries: part II. Fractures, dislocations, and thumb injuries. Am Fam Physician 2006;73:827–834.
